utterances.text: I moved around. I was in this room, but I was also on the ground floor, here (indicating), because there was a toilet here that we all used, on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In the course of that day, therefore, you found refuge in the room that we see the door of on photograph number 6, and also from time to time you went up to the ground floor because the toilet was there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you show us or tell us the people who were with you in the room that we see on photograph number 6? Of course, if you can remember that. Which other families found refuge in that same room?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were many people there. It is difficult to remember all those people, because people were going up and down, moving around. But I can remember, for instance, some of those families. There was Nevenka Marjanovic, with her children; she had a small baby in those days. Then there was Lucinka Papic; she had five children. Then Jela Vidovic, a sick woman, whom they carried in on a stretcher. Then I saw Ruza Grgic there as well. All these rooms were full, so it is hard to recollect all those names, but I shall try, if necessary, to recall some other names.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You told us yesterday, madam, that your husband, Vlatko Kupreskic, stayed with you in the basement, in the room that you have shown us, until about 10.00 in the morning. You confirmed that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I draw your attention to the fact, madam, that two witnesses who testified here -- you wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I thought you had finished your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Well, answer the question that you thought I had put to you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Vlatko came with us that morning, but he didn't stay for a long time in the basement because there were a lot of women and children, so he went back upstairs to the ground floor. I, too, didn't spend a long time in this room. I went upstairs often to smoke a cigarette.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Why, madam, did your husband leave this house about 10.00 in the morning, according to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He left the house because the shooting had subsided and because everyone around him was saying that he should go and check how his father was, whom we had left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When you left your house that morning, were you disturbed about what could happen to your father-in-law, and was your husband, too, worried about what could happen to his father?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When we left the house, we had no idea that anything could happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But nevertheless, madam, you left your house before 6.00 in great haste because you received warnings and advice, strong advice, to go to a shelter. You must have thought that there was a risk to stay on in that house.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I repeat again. If Ivica Kupreskic hadn't called up, we would have stayed in our house. What was decisive for us to leave was Ivica Kupreskic's call.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I understand that, madam. Ivica Kupreskic called you up, and you decided to leave. But if you decided to leave, it is because you thought or, rather, Ivica Kupreskic convinced you that it was risky to stay in that house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. The very thought of the word "Mujahedin" caused fear, and we were afraid to stay in the house, because this wasn't the first time that we fled our house. But we couldn't imagine that that morning, anything could happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Madam, I would like you to be very precise in expressing your thoughts. You have just told us that the very word "Mujahedin" frightened you. You left your house with your children, your husband, your mother-in-law. Isn't it reasonable to think that if you left that house, it was because you thought that there was a danger in staying in that house that morning; isn't that reasonable, to conclude that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, whether it's reasonable or not, I don't know. When Ivica called up, saying that everyone had left and sought shelter, why would we stay on?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'm trying to clarify why you left behind you your father-in-law. Wasn't there some way, any way, of taking him with you as far as the shelter, as Mirjan Kupreskic did for his own mother-in-law, if I remember well, who was transported in a wheelbarrow, I think? Wasn't there any way to ensure the safety of your father-in-law?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Because Vlatko's father didn't want to leave, and he was a sick man. Even then, we thought it was a mere provocation and nothing would come of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In your opinion, could you explain why your father-in-law, Vlatko's father, did not wish to leave?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's not that he didn't wish to leave. He couldn't leave because he was sick. However, later when we got together, he said that if he had known what would happen, he would have crawled on all fours to leave the house. I remember that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When did you see him again, your father-in-law?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I saw him that same day on the 16th of April, in the evening about 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I saw him when Vlatko arrived and brought him here to this room in the ground floor. At first, he was here somewhere. Then he was in this other room where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In your opinion, your father-in-law, Vlatko's father, as soon as he realised it was not a provocation but something very serious, that is, after 5.30, couldn't he have joined you before 8.00 in the evening in the shelter where you were?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was hard to bring a man who carried a stick, who had an operated hip, who breathes with difficulty. It was hard for him to reach the shelter on foot. In the meantime, there was shooting going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But he did so, nevertheless, in the evening, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Madam, do you remember writing a letter to the Prosecutor of this Tribunal in November 1997?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a copy of that letter.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is Exhibit 361.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Is that the letter that you wrote to the Prosecutor of this Tribunal in November 1997?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I draw your attention, madam, to the top of the second page of the English version, I think it is the same spot in the Bosnian version, where you say that your husband, Vlatko, who was with you in the shelter, received orders to go to Niko Sakic's house, where he was detailed to help the wounded, where he had to treat the wounded. Your husband, according to what you wrote, received orders to go to Niko Sakic's house to take care of the wounded?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is not correct, because this is just a summary of my story, my statement before Grlimir Jonjic, who is a relative of my husband's.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Madam, this is a letter that you addressed to the Prosecutor of this Tribunal in The Hague in November 1997, and you wrote in that letter, which I think was written freely, unless you deny it, that your husband, who was in the shelter, received orders to go and care for the wounded?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is what I was told then, but that is not true because I was against Vlatko's leaving the shelter. I grew up without a father. I was an orphan. I was afraid that Vlatko would get killed, and I was told that he was ordered to go to Niko Sakic's house. And then I realised, afterwards only, the truth, that Vlatko had gone home to see what was happening with his father.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I don't understand anymore. You tell us that your husband, Vlatko, was with you all the time in the shelter next to the Vrebacs, and now you tell us that he left. But you must have learned when he left, if you were present, and if he were present, you must have known why he left.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. He was there until 10.00. He left around 10.00. I learned the real truth, that he had gone to see if his father was alive. But for that, this gentleman who typed this thing did not write that. I mean how could Vlatko extend aid to the injured when he was an economist, a graduate economist? He's not a physician. I mean it's nonsense but there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Well, it may not be nonsense, because somebody else brought it to the Tribunal. Was it Sakic who --

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, that's what I remember being told, because I was really against Vlatko's going back home. I was afraid he would get killed, and that is why I was told what I was told. Only when Vlatko came back did I find out that he had gone home and that his father was alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you please try to be as clear as possible, because this is a very important point. So let us be very clear. You said today, and I'm listening to you now, it seems that you were not present -- that you weren't next to him at the moment when Vlatko left the shelter.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was present 100 per cent when Vlatko left, because who else would he have addressed if not me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But at that moment as he was leaving the shelter, did he tell you then why he was going out and where he was going?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He told me then that he had been ordered, because he saw me crying, I was afraid, and that he had been ordered to go to Niko Sakic's house. But after he found his father alive in the house and when he returned, it was then that he told me the truth, that in fact he had gone home to see his father.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So as your husband, Vlatko Kupreskic, leaves the shelter, he tells you that he had been issued orders to take care of the wounded?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was his uncle who told me that he had received those orders. It was Anto Kupreskic or, rather, Vlatko's father's brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I am asking about what Vlatko Kupreskic said.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, Vlatko said that he would like to go home and see if his father was alive. But as I was against it, at that time Vlatko's uncle said that he should go to Niko Sakic's house and extend aid to the injured. I thought at that time that that was the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But did you ask your husband to confirm it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But wasn't his feeling of duty, to go and see his father to see if he was still alive, wasn't that a sufficient reason for him to leave? Did he really need to have an order to go and attend to the wounded for you to let him go?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Because I was crying, I was afraid that he would get killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Then why, when you wrote this letter to the Prosecutor of the Tribunal, why didn't you simply say that your husband, Vlatko Kupreskic, left the shelter at 10.00 in the morning because he wanted to go and see whether his father was still alive? Why didn't you say that quite simply in that letter?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, first let me explain how this letter was written and who did it, because it wasn't me who typed it. I told the whole story, how it happened and what happened on the 16th of April, 1993, and this letter was typed by Grlimir Jonjic, Vlatko's relative, Vlatko's cousin, who can be called to testify if need be. So there are some changes here. There is a date which is wrong here. And I did not read that letter again after it was typed. So on the basis of my story, he wrote this letter, and all these enclosures that I gave him, he enclosed here attached to this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let me just comment. You seem to me quite a temperamental woman, I realise that, but let me tell you that you're running an enterprise with about a dozen persons, they seem to be properly looked after, and I simply refuse to believe that in a case of such gravity and concerning the family so much, you simply failed to read again a letter which you were sending and -- a letter to the Prosecutor of the Tribunal, which you then signed. I find it difficult to believe that you didn't go through it.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: But this is not my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just a moment ago, you identified the letter.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did identify the summary of the letter. I know that that is the letter. But the signature -- I never read this letter. It was Mr. Grlimir who called me from Sarajevo and told me that the letter had been typed and could he sign it in my name, and I told him he could because I thought that he had written -- that he had taken down our conversation and typed it there. But if this letter is at issue, we could call this gentleman to testify here. He's there and he's alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, that would be highly advisable indeed. But let us understand your position just a moment ago, that as a matter of fact this was the letter that you sent to the Prosecutor. Now you said that you entrusted it to a cousin or a friend, to an individual that you entrusted the drafting of this letter which was, as a matter of fact, your personal letter to the Prosecutor. You let somebody else then write it. Now you tell us you never even read it, never even signed it, but it was signed by somebody else in your name. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Quite. I did not sign this letter. I never had an opportunity to read it. All I was informed is that on the basis of my whole story and the documents here, that this letter was drafted on the basis of all that, then typed and sent to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Therefore, it is quite possible, if I am to believe you, it can --

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So can one take it then that in this letter, very few things are truthful, because after what you are telling us, it is possible that this letter contains all sorts of errors and mistakes, according to your statements?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. Here there are a couple, only, of errors, but the rest of it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you please show us your signature, a specimen of your signature?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: No, no, that's not what I want. I'm asking if you have any document with your signature. I'm not asking you to sign now a new document. Do you have something which carries your signature? Do you have a contract, your identity document or something, something which bears your signature? Do you have anything with you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Witness complies)

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Well, as this is not your signature, does it mean that you are seeing this document for the first time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, this is not the first time I've seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When did you first see this document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When it was submitted to you, to the international police in Sarajevo, I was then given a copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you read it then? Did you look into what that document contained, the one that you were given a copy of?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yeah, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Weren't you surprised by the errors that you found in it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, this letter should have been much more exhaustive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I mean that this whole event, our departure, our stay, our return, should have -- it should have taken many more pages. This is just a summary of our conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But why didn't you then take care that this letter be complete, be rounded off?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, we thought that all these documents which were sent would show clearly enough that Vlatko Kupreskic was a war invalid, that he had a university diploma, that he was a businessman, that he had been on a business trip on the eve of the conflict, and a number of other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'd like you to tell me, what do you think about the following: We know, through different contacts which you had with some of the prosecution witnesses -- and I'm just mentioning it, but we know that there were some contacts; we know the importance that you are attaching to the defence of your husband. And I think it only natural, of course. I would not bear a grudge against you for that. What surprises me is this casual attitude that you showed with regard to this letter that was sent to the Prosecutor, and this carelessness which you permitted when you allowed somebody else to sign this letter in your name, because legally speaking, it is then a forgery.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, that is not true, really. I wasn't then involved in my husband's defence so much at that time as I am today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I should also like to hear your response to the following: We heard here Niko Sakic testify. Could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: If you have more questions on the same --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, I will come back to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: This Court heard the testimony of Niko Sakic, and he knew your husband at that time, and he said that your husband was that night to take care of the wounded, but that that night -- there were no wounded that night, so it must have -- but according to this witness, your husband's duty was to take care of the wounded. That is what he told this Court. Now, what is your response to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I did not hear that witness say that here, and I'd like this to be checked in the transcript, but I do not remember that witness saying that. I may be wrong, and I will apologise if I am, but I do not remember that witness saying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could make a break in order to check whether Niko Sakic did indeed say that. 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'm referring to page 8.298 of the transcript. This is the cross-examination of Niko Sakic, a Defence witness. I'll give you the gist of it. This is for Mr. Par: The Prosecutor is asking of Mr. Sakic whether the latter remembers making a statement, a written statement, in January 1998, which statement was disclosed to the Prosecution. Mr. Sakic states, in this written statement disclosed to the Prosecution by the Defence, that around 10.00 in the morning, Vlatko Kupreskic appeared in front of the witness's house because, according to what the witness understood, he was detailed to help evacuate the wounded. Vlatko allegedly stayed there for about three hours, and since there were no wounded, he then left. When faced with this written statement, the witness, testifying before the Tribunal, stated that he then thought the following: Since Vlatko Kupreskic was not fit for active military service, since he was not a member of an army or a political or social organisation, and because he had a driving license, he was bound to provide medical aid. The witness specified that these were his own thoughts. This was his own opinion. I was referring to this very statement, and I'd like the witness to tell us whether the statement which I've just mentioned and the mention we found in the letter to the Prosecutor of this Tribunal do not call for some observations from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't want to cause any particular problems, but we checked the notes regarding Sakic's testimony, and it emerges from our notes that in answer to the Prosecutor's question, explaining his previous statement, he said that he thought that for those reasons Vlatko Kupreskic was there, to care for the wounded; and after that, in continuation of his testimony, he said that Vlatko told him the real reason. I really do not wish to prevent the Prosecutor in any way asking this question, and to clear it up, I'm just against anyone saying explicitly that this was something that Witness Sakic had explicitly stated. So could this question be rephrased so as not to cause any debate or dispute over it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to rephrase the question, but basically in the same words, because I thought that my question was perfectly in keeping with the statement made by Niko Sakic, which I tried to reproduce the most exactly and the most honestly possible. The witness said that when he saw Vlatko Kupreskic turn up at the threshold of his house, this witness thought that Vlatko Kupreskic, given the circumstances I have alluded to, was detailed to help the wounded. That was the witness's personal statement which he transcribed in a written statement dated January 1998, a statement taken by the Defence and disclosed by the Defence to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So my question to the witness is as follows: Isn't it strange, is there no explanation to be provided for the fact that Niko Sakic thought what he thought when he saw Vlatko Kupreskic on the 16th of April, around 10.00 in the morning, according to the witness, and to the fact that we find in the written letter, a letter written in October 1997 to the Prosecutor, which gives us the same account, the same explanation for Vlatko's departure from the shelter. Is there no explanation to be given for this coincidence, let us say?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Niko Sakic, why he thought that, I cannot know. Niko Sakic probably couldn't think of anything else because he didn't know that his father was at home. That is one thing. Secondly, I was told that this was the case, but when Vlatko returned, he told me that he had gone home to see how his father was doing, because I was absolutely opposed to him going.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Would you please explain to me why, if Vlatko Kupreskic was indeed worried about his father, why then, after taking his family to the Vrebacs' shelter, after making sure that all the family members were safe there, why he didn't straightaway return to see his father close to the house? Why did he wait four hours to do so, four hours, from 6.00 until 10.00?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: First of all, Vlatko is not a very healthy man. He's afraid when he hears shooting. And secondly, the father was at home, and there was less danger of him being shot or hit by a bullet than for Vlatko, who would be moving through open space.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Can you give me another explanation, madam? If indeed Vlatko was worried about his father, if that is the reason why he left the shelter, the Vrebac shelter at 10.00, why, according to Niko Sakic's testimony, he stayed at Niko Sakic's from 10.30 until 12.30 or 1.00, so basically from 10.00 until 12.30; why did he stay there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't understand. Where did he stay?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: At the house of Niko Sakic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot know the details as to why he stayed there, but I know when he returned to the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us why you are so absolutely certain of the time when Vlatko Kupreskic left the Vrebacs' shelter?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sure because I know, and this is what I remember in particular, my son Igor started vomiting in the basement, so I took him upstairs to the ground floor. Vlatko was there, and I took the boy to the toilet, and Vlatko took him in his lap. In the meantime, I ran across to Jozo Vrebac's house and made tea for the boy, and I know it was around 10.00, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you have a watch?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did have a watch on my wrist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Are you sure of the time when Vlatko Kupreskic returned to the shelter?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon when he came back. He brought with him some bread and salami because it was time for lunch, and we were hungry, and there was nothing in the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea -- you possibly can't remember, but do you have any idea of the time when he came back to the shelter?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it could have been about 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In other words, your husband, according to your statement, was absent from 10.00 to 4.00 in the afternoon. That is, altogether, six hours. Did he tell you what he had done during those six hours?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What did he tell you he did?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He said that he had stayed for a while in Niko Sakic's house, that the shooting had started again, and that he couldn't go to our house. Then he reached our house and he stayed with his father for a short time. He picked up the food for us, and he returned to Samija Kata and Niko Sakic house because they started shooting again, and he took shelter there too for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Just an observation. Your husband, Vlatko Kupreskic, said that he spent some time in the house of Niko Sakic, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, but I should like to intervene on account of the transcript. The witness said that he returned to Kata and Nikola Samija's house, and in the transcript it says "Samija Kata and Niko Sakic". This is an error in the transcript. The name is Kata and Nikola Samija. This is one house owned by these two people, so this question put by the Prosecutor is also wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I stand to be corrected by Ms. Slokovic-Glumac, but the witness did say that Vlatko Kupreskic said that he spent some time in Niko Sakic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: This is indeed what your husband told you he did?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, when he left the shelter, and not on the way back from our house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So as he left the shelter. This is indeed what Niko Sakic testified before this Tribunal. I fail to understand, because when I was quoting Niko Sakic, you seemed surprise, and you affirmed and you said that you didn't know anything about it. So I'll repeat my question, because it was unanswered before. Didn't you think it was strange that your husband leaving the shelter in order to see about his father, since he was worried about him, that your husband should stay to spend some time in Niko Sakic's house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not surprised, because there was probably shooting, so he couldn't go to our house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Towards the end of the afternoon, when you saw your husband again, did he tell you that during those six hours outside the shelter, that he met, for instance, Ivica Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Zoran Kupreskic, Mirko Sakic; did he mention those names?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that he met Niko Sakic. I don't know about any of the others. He didn't tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: We know about Niko Sakic. I was thinking of Mirko Sakic, Ivica Kupreskic, Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic. I could also mention Milutin Vidovic, Jozo Alilovic. Did he meet all these people? Did he mention meeting all these people?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On that day, the 16th of April, no, he didn't mention them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When he returned to the shelter in the afternoon, as you said, around 4.00 in the afternoon, was he together with his father?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Under which circumstances did his father arrive then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: His father arrived towards nightfall. Actually, it was already dark. I remember that well. It was around 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did the father come alone?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He came with Vlatko. Vlatko went back to the house again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'm now moving on to the ensuing period, the period following the 16th of April. I have a few questions in this respect. You told us that following the 16th of April, you became refugees. Thereon, you showed us a certificate which is D41/3. What does the word "refugees" mean if it's used in this type of certificate which was issued by the social services in Vitez? What does the word "refugees" mean in this context?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In that context, the word "refugee" means that we are not living or residing in our own home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When did you see your house again in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I saw my house in Ahmici again for the first time ten days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When did you occupy again that house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 1st of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When did your husband start working again?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He started working again when we moved to Vitez, when we became refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you remember the date, the approximate date if need be, on which your husband started working again in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When we left Donja Rovna.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: That is how many days after the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think 10 or 15 days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So between the 26th of April and the end of the month of April; is that so? Is it then that he resumed his professional activities?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: As far as you can remember, when did the Sutre store start working again, the one that is close to your house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: After the 16th of April? I didn't quite understand what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You told us that 10 to 15 days following the 16th of April, your husband started working again in Vitez. I would like you now to specify around what time after the 16th of April this store, the Sutre store, opened again.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In Pirici, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Pirici.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: After the cease-fire was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you be more specific as to the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The beginning of May 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So to make things clear, early May 1994, at the latest, that is when your husband's professional activities and, I suppose, also Ivica Kupreskic's professional activities resumed in Vitez and in Pirici; is that so? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: After the truce was signed at the beginning of May 1994, both Vlatko and Ivica continued their private businesses both in Vitez and in Pirici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In Pirici, things were safe enough, I suppose, from a military point of view, safe enough for professional activities to be happening without any particular risk attached to this?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In what period? After the truce was signed?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: At the time when your husband's professional activities were resumed in Pirici, for instance, that is, in early May. I withdraw the question. There was confusion on my part as to the date which you had mentioned. Here's another question for you, madam: You told us that you saw your house again some ten days after the 16th of April. I'm not wrong in saying that, am I?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What condition was the house in?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In a chaotic state.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: "Chaotic"? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When I arrived home, when I saw the door that had been broken in by force, when I saw a lot of mud in the house and the earth from the flowerpots -- which confirms what Vlatko's father said, that they were looking for money -- when I saw my clothes and Vlatko's clothes strewn all over the place, in the house and in the rooms and in the living room, I was astonished. There were cigarettes that had been extinguished on the carpet. My handbag was in a corner, and all documents -- or rather the document that was valid for transportation in those days, with my photograph on it, my name and surname, I remember that very well -- had fallen out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So what you are describing there is damage caused, say, by robbery; these are not materiel damage caused by explosives or bullets hitting the house? And I'm seeking confirmation from you: Your house was not hit by firearms, by war weapons?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was damage on the facade that can be visible to this day, and on the tiles, too, but the tiles have been changed. And the windowpanes had been broken. But we've changed all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Back at the time, were there any photographs made of the damage? Did you take stock of the damage caused to the house?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We compiled a report. When the commission was set up for war damages I applied, and this can be seen from the document in '95.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Are you talking about a report, a specific document, or is this part of the documents that were handed in to the Tribunal beforehand, a document dated the 5th of April, 1995, which is damage caused to a building on the 5th of April, 1995? Is that the document you have in mind, or do you have anything else?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is the document which registers the war damage inflicted on the 16th of April, 1993. A commission went on the spot and established on site the damage done to the house and made a normal record of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, Mr. Par submitted two documents, or mentioned two documents and submitted one of them. It is a document marked 12A/3, dated 5th of April, 1993, which very briefly mentions a certain amount of damage. There is another document, dated the 21st of January, 1999, mentioning a robbery in the family house of the Kupreskics on the 7th of May, 1994. During that robbery, damage was caused to the front door and to the balcony. Given the situation, isn't it logical to think that the damage registered in the report of the 5th of April, 1995 -- I'm not challenging this fact -- was caused by the robbery you were a victim of in 1994, and that the damage has nothing to do with the events of the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm going to explain it to you. The first burglary in my house, it wasn't that the burglars came through the door; they came over the balcony, they climbed the balcony and entered the loft. They never used the entrance door, and that is 100 per cent certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'm merely referring to the certificate, madam, as established by the police services in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was the attempt. The thief tried to enter through the main door but failed. I don't know how to explain it to you that our entrance door, our main door, has now been so reinforced that nobody can enter it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'm not interested in knowing where the thief went through. I say that on the basis of the certificate, on the 17th of May, 1994, around 3.45, your house was burgled by an unidentified person, and during the burglary, visible damage was caused to the front door as well as to the balcony door, but during that burglary, nothing was stolen from the house. There was only damage to the front door of the house and to the door of the balcony. Hence, my question: I'm wondering whether the record of damage, as established much later, nearly a year later, does not merely refer to what had been caused during that burglary?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't understand you again. Could you please help me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'm only too pleased to do so, madam. First of all, you submitted a certificate by the Vitez police according to which, on the 17th of May, 1994, there was an attempted burglary during which damage was caused to the front door and to the balcony door of your family house. Secondly, we also have a document entitled "Record of Damage on a Building on the 15th of April, 1995," and in this document there is indeed an indication of damage caused basically to what was in stock and store in the shop. So I'm wondering as to whether what is registered, what is recorded in 1995, has anything do with what happened in April 1993. Did you not, as a matter of fact -- or do you have any evidence that there was damage caused to your house in April 1993? Have I been clear enough this time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You have proof. Isn't the commission which came out to establish the war damage and the commission -- and what do we call it -- the crime department, they come on behalf of the police, they come out, they conduct an on-site investigation and make a record of the burglary, they take fingerprints and then take note of all that. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: One last question before moving on to another topic. The question arising here is to find out whether you have any evidence of damage caused to your house in April '93. What is the evidence you have, what evidence can you tender to this Tribunal showing that there was damage made to your house on the 16th of April, 1993? This is the very question I want to put to you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the front door is a proof, because that is how it was. Proof is Vlatko's briefcase, which you also had here, and one could see how it was damaged. I had completely forgotten about it, but one could see that it had also been forced open.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: One very last question before moving on. You say that damage was caused to your house. What is the evidence you can bring for that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I've just listed them. Besides, there are also bills which were filed, and we see what kind of merchandise, what kind of things were taken away. And as for evidence, well, this commission which was there, and persons who are on the witness list, they came out, and they could see the damage done to my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So you have in mind the commission which took stock on the 5th of April, 1995, but I have another question for you. A military from the British battalion testified before this Tribunal and said the following -- this is page 2.634 of the transcript. He was Corporal Skillen. Corporal Skillen said to this Tribunal -- and I stand to be corrected by Mr. Par if need be -- he said that in April, '93, he entered the village of Ahmici, he had left his vehicle next to the mosque, and that he then moved up to the top of the village. He walked up to the top of the village, and at a certain point in time his attention was drawn to a house, which he very precisely described, and which he indicated on the aerial photograph. It ensues from the explanation provided to the Tribunal by this witness, beyond any ambiguity, that this house which his attention was attracted to was yours. He noticed your house, he said, because, given the chaotic environment -- there were still bodies, corpses, lying around in certain houses in the village -- because in the balcony of that house he noticed a woman and a child. When he passed by again, passed by that house again, on that very balcony, there was still the woman and the child as well as two other people. Here's my question: Were you the woman that that soldier saw on that balcony?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you have any explanation why that English military saw this woman?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I really don't understand. I know we went back to the house ten days later, and I was crying so much when I saw it, when I saw all the houses that had burned down. When I got to my house, when I saw what had happened to it, and when I took some few clothes for the children, then some foreign journalists came up, and they wanted to record us. And that I was on the balcony, that is simply not true. At that time we were still in Donja Rovna. That was April '93.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The time that I have in mind is the 22nd of April, 1993, according to the witness's statement, before the foreign journalists were there. Do you have any idea who might have been there, who that woman was and who that child was who were on the balcony?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't. Afterwards, I heard that they even needed a van to take away all of the clothes stocked in our house, in the cellar. Perhaps somebody entered my house without my knowledge. I do not know that. But I claim the full responsibility that I was not there. And what would I be doing on the balcony at that time of the year? It's cold in Bosnia in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How old were your children then, in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My son was 6 and my daughter 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: One moment, please. I have no further questions. I thank the witness. I'm only asking for Exhibits 359, 360, and 361 to be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any objection? No objection? Thank you. So they are admitted into evidence. Counsel Par? We still have 16 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, actually, I have a question for the witness. Madam, I know that you are tired, and I apologise, but I have a very minor and brief question: In your letter to the International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, on page 2, you mention a book. You say, and I will slowly read it in English: "I would like to refer you," you say to the Prosecutor, "to the book 'Time of Dishonour - the genocide against the Bosniaks in the 20th century,' published by a group of authors in Zenica in 1994, and especially to its offprint, 'The Tragedy in the Lasva Valley - statements of victims, pages 153-161' by the author Ragib Hadzic, which discusses the perpetrators of the crime in Ahmici." Could you please tell us about this book, and in particular the chapter written by the author, Hadzic, about the crime in Ahmici? You seem to be familiar with this book, and so I was keen to know something about this particular book, because to the best of my knowledge, it has not been presented to the Court as a piece of evidence. You also say, later on, the authors of that book "know very well the situation in the Lasva Valley."

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you for your question. It is true that I did read the book at the time when the letter was written. As far as I know, it was Vlatko's aunt's book; she lives in Zenica. I believe that book was sent to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So you, yourself, you have not read that book, so you are simply --

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did, I did read it, but not all of it, just fragments, because it describes all of the plight of the Lasva Valley, not only in Ahmici, and events in Ahmici are not in -- there is not a single line in that book referring to what happened in Ahmici that would mention the name of my husband. That is as far as I recollect, but I did not really read the book through, because it is quite a volume, and it describes all the trials and tribulations of the people in the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, but I mean, I understand from your reference to your husband that in at least one chapter of this book a description is made of what happened in Ahmici, and probably this is based on statements of victims. So I, for one, would be interested in seeing what those victims state, because I understand from your letter that they do mention names of possible perpetrators, and your point is that however, among those names, one cannot find the name of your husband. So therefore it might have some interest. Anyway, I wonder whether the parties may be of some assistance in this -- yes, Counsel Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I believe we have the book, and we shall try to send it to the Tribunal or, rather, have translated that part which refers to Ahmici and give it to the Prosecution. I believe we had a copy here in The Hague. If that is indeed so, then the Court will have it in no time at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any further questions. All right. Mrs. Kupreskic, thank you so much for giving evidence in court. I assume all other parties do not object to your being released. You may now be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Since it is fairly late, we will resume tomorrow at 9.00 sharp. However, tomorrow we have to stop at half past 12.00, at the request of the Registrar. The Registry needs this courtroom, so we can't but bow to her request, so therefore we have only a limited amount of hours, from 9.00 to half past 12.00. Tomorrow is Thursday, but on Friday, of course, we will resume at 9.00 until 1.30. All right. So the hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 1.18 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 27th day of May, 1999, at 9.00 a.m.
